data.title: Healthcare transparency
data.description: Recently, several Federal laws have been enacted that require group health plans to make certain health care cost information available publicly so that…
data.content: Recently, several Federal laws have been enacted that require group health plans to make certain health care cost information available publicly so that consumers can better understand the costs associated with health care. The information is designed to help consumers know the cost for services they receive from doctors, hospitals and other health care providers before receiving the care. This information contained on this page is designed to comply with these Federal laws. Transparency in coverage In 2020, the Federal Government finalized the “Transparency in Coverage” rule, which is intended to make health care pricing more accessible and understandable for consumers. The Transparency in Coverage Rule requires health insurers and group health plans, including self-funded plans, to provide cost-sharing data to consumers via two different methods, machine-readable files and an online consumer price transparency tool. Machine-readable files Machine-readable files must be published for plan years beginning on or after July 1, 2022 and provide pricing data for covered items and services (in-network negotiated payment rates, historical out-of-network allowed amounts, and historical costs). Information in these files must be updated monthly. Machine-readable files for Prescription drug rates will be required at a later date to be determined by the Federal Government. To link to the machine-readable files for Aetna, please click this link for the Railroad Employees National Health and Welfare Plan - https://Health1.Aetna.com/app/public/#/one/insurerCode=AETNACVS_I&brandCode=ALICSI/machine-readable-transparency-in-coverage?searchTerm=267180&lock=true or click this link for The SMART-TD Health and Welfare Plan - https://Health1.Aetna.com/app/public/#/one/insurerCode=AETNACVS_I&brandCode=ALICSI/machine-readable-transparency-in-coverage?searchTerm=188989&lock=true To link to the machine-readable files for Highmark BlueCross Blue Shield, please click on this link: mrfdata.hmhs.com To link to the machine-readable files for UnitedHealthcare, please click on this link: https://transparency-in-coverage.uhc.com/ Consumer price transparency tool: This online tool for members will include personalized, real-time, cost-share estimates for covered services and items, including prescription information, with paper versions available upon request. The tool will be available for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2023 for 500 designated services and plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2024 for all services. Links to the tool for each medical benefits administrator will be posted by January 1, 2023. Surprise medical billing notice Part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act (the “CAA”) passed by the Federal government in 2020, establishes standards to protect consumers from “surprise” bills or balance billing for certain items and services provided by specified doctors, hospitals and air ambulance carriers on an out-of-network (OON) basis. These “Surprise Bills” apply only to covered medical bills related to: Out-of-Network emergency services at a hospital/freestanding facility. Items and services provided by certain out-of-network health care providers at an in-network facility. Out-of-network air ambulance items and services. Please click on this link to read the Surprise Medical Billing Notice: Surprise Medical Bill Notice

data.title: Tips to make the most of benefits
data.description: Are you and your family getting the most out of your health and wellness benefits?
data.content: Seven ways to use benefits to your advantage Seven ways to use benefits to your advantage Are you and your family getting the most out of your health and wellness benefits? Empower yourself and your loved ones by learning more about the resources available to you. 1. PROTECT YOURSELF AND YOUR FAMILY According to the CDC, more than 100,000 deaths could be prevented each year if people received preventive care. That’s why we believe preventive health is so important. Your Railroad medical plan covers recommended Affordable Care Act (ACA) preventive health services 100% when you use an in-network provider. Curious which services are covered for your family? Call your medical vendor . 2. SAVE TIME AND MONEY ON MEDICATIONS Optum Rx works with your plan to help you get the medication you need. Use your online account to view your prescription ID card, set up home delivery, find a nearby network pharmacy and much more. Have questions about a prescription? Call Optum Rx Member Services 24/7, 1-844-368-8736, TTY 711. 3. PAY LESS BY USING IN-NETWORK SERVICE When you use in-network providers for medical, dental, vision and behavioral health , you’ll benefit from the lowest out-of-pocket costs. While using out-of-network providers is always an option, please know that you will end up paying more out of pocket. Wondering if your provider is in-network? Call your dental, vision, medical or behavioral health administrator . 4. ACCESS MENTAL HEALTH RESOURCES AVAILABLE TO YOU Relationship issues, daily responsibilities at work and other factors can affect your emotional health. If you or a loved one is feeling overwhelmed or finding it difficult to cope with stressful situations, it may be time to talk to a professional. Not sure where to start? Call United Behavioral Health 24/7 to speak privately with a professional, 1-866-850-6212. HELPFUL NOTE: If seeking services on your own, be sure to verify that the provider is in-network. 5. TAKE ADVANTAGE OF EXPERT COACHING SERVICES Railroad HEALTHLINK offers wellness coaching for you and your family. You can work privately with a coach to create a simple plan to exercise more, eat better, quit smoking, reduce stress and more. Plans can be customized based on your schedule, budget and fitness level. Interested in a personalized plan? Call Railroad HEALTHLINK at 1-866-735-5685 or click here to get started today. 6. GET QUALITY-RATED CARE You and your family deserve the very best. Your medical insurance company can help you check quality (and cost-efficiency) measures on numerous physicians, facilities and/or specialties. Prefer a provider rated for quality? Call your medical vendor . 7. SAVE ON HEALTH CARE-RELATED EXPENSES WITH AN FSA Contributing to a health flexible spending account (FSA) allows you to save pre-tax dollars while putting aside money for eligible health care expenses. Each year, you can sign up during open enrollment (October 1–31) to select the amount of money you want to contribute from each paycheck in the year ahead. Want more info? Click here to learn more. data.description: From where to go for care to treatment options, call 24/7 Nurses & Health Specialists for answers and support.

Talk with a nurse for guidance on managing back or joint pain, understanding treatment options and navigating orthopedic surgical care with help from a Lantern Care Advocate. Managing a health condition? Our nurses can help you manage ongoing health conditions such as heart disease, diabetes and asthma. Diagnosed with cancer? Our oncology nurses can help you explore treatment options and navigate the physical and emotional challenges. Questions about COVID-19? If you have questions or need support, our nurses are standing by to help you and your family, around the clock. Additional 24/7 nurses & health specialist support Confidential health and wellness support for Railroad employees and their families at no additional cost. 24/7 telemedicine 24/7 access to doctors Teladoc’s U.S. board-certified doctors are available 24/7 to provide care for non-emergency conditions like the flu, bronchitis, allergies, eczema, and much more. Your eligible dependents can also receive on-demand care. Register now , so you and your dependents won’t have to wait when care is needed. With Teladoc, any general medical appointment will cost you $10 or less. You can schedule a visit wherever you are, whenever you need it, through the Teladoc app, online, or over the phone. For non-emergency issues, Teladoc visits are less expensive than trips to the ER, urgent care, or primary care physician’s office. Getting started Talk to a Teladoc doctor within minutes through the Teladoc app, website, or by calling 800-Teladoc (835-2362). You already have Teladoc as part of your benefits. To get started download the Teladoc app , visit the member portal , or call to create your account and quickly complete your medical history. Once that is complete, you can will have the ability to schedule a visit whenever you need it through your device, computer, or over the phone. Medical treatments and services from trusted physicians Last year, Teladoc connected its members to experienced doctors for 2.6 million visits. Teladoc’s U.S. board-certified doctors average 20 years of experience and are credentialed every three years, meeting NCQA standards. Use Teladoc for non-emergency issues and to be treated for conditions such as cold & flu symptoms, allergies, sinus problems, sore throat, respiratory infection, skin problems, and much more. If needed, Teladoc doctors can even write prescriptions and have them sent directly to your local pharmacy. With your consent, a Teladoc doctor can electronically send a write-up of your visit to your primary care physician. Behavioral health treatments and services from trusted clinicians Get counseling seven days a week for conditions like depression, anxiety, stress, family issues, and much more. Choose the therapist or psychiatrist who best fits your needs and set an appointment around your schedule. Use confidential treatment for as little or as long as you need. data.content: Keeping you updated Important things to know about COVID-19 24/7 Nurses & Health Specialists are here to provide straight answers to your COVID-19 questions and ongoing, dedicated support around the clock: 1-866-735-5685. Should I get tested? If you experience any of the common COVID-19 symptoms, a nurse can help you decide if you should make an appointment with your doctor or seek available testing. Is COVID-19 vaccine safe? Yes, it is safe. Even though this vaccine was developed quickly, precautions were not overlooked. After large clinical trials to test safety and effectiveness, scientists confirmed the vaccines meet the strict standards set by the Food & Drug Administration (FDA). 1 Where do I go to get vaccinated? Each state has its own vaccination priority plan. For information about when and where you can get vaccinated, visit your state health department website. Find the link to your state here . No matter where you go to get the COVID-19 vaccine, your Railroad health and welfare benefits have you covered. Administrative costs to get the vaccine are covered by the Medical Plans and/or by the Prescription Drug Plan, so you will not pay a copay, deductible or coinsurance for any of the doses that are required. If you go to your clinic or doctor to get vaccinated, present your Medical Plan ID card (from Aetna, Highmark or UnitedHealthcare). * If you get vaccinated at your local pharmacy, present either your Medical Plan ID card or your Express Scripts ® Prescription ID card. Learn more Or call 24/7 Nurses & Health Specialists at 1-866-735-5685. * If you get vaccinated during a regular office visit, the visit will be covered according to your medical plan benefits. Coverage of the COVID-19 vaccine is subject to federal regulation during the public health emergency period. Once the public health emergency period ends, coverage for the COVID-19 vaccine may be modified by the plan. 1 U.S. Food & Drug Administration. November 2020.

data.title: Enroll now for 2014
data.description: The Health FSA Benefit for Railroad Members — Enroll Now for 2014
data.content: The Health FSA Benefit for Railroad Members — Enroll Now for 2014 Watch a short video to learn more about a health FSA. A health flexible spending account (FSA) is a benefit plan that lets you save money by putting pre-tax money aside in a special account to help pay for certain medical costs and other eligible health services . This means you can save on what you pay in your annual income taxes. New for 2014 — A Health FSA Debit Card When you enroll in the health FSA for 2014, you will be able to use a special debit card to easily pay for eligible FSA expenses. It’s connected to your flexible spending account so there’s no need to write checks or submit claim forms. Look for more information in the future that explains how your debit card may help you manage your out of pocket expenses. How it works When you enroll in a health FSA, a specific amount of money, based on what you decide to contribute annually during Open Enrollment, is withdrawn from your paycheck and placed in your account. This money is withdrawn before taxes are calculated. You can decide to contribute as little as $10 per month ($120 annually) or as much as $208.33 per month ($2,500 annually). See the health FSA Summary Plan Description for more plan details. Calculate your potential savings Use the FSA calculator to see the potential tax savings you and your family could experience with a health FSA. See Grace's savings example below: Grace and her family enroll in a health FSA and decide to contribute $2,000 annually ($166.67 per month) to the FSA to pay for the family's doctors' visits, prescriptions, new eyeglasses and contact lenses. Based on Grace's annual tax obligations, she and her family could save more than $900 in taxes a year by enrolling in and contributing $2,000 annually to a health FSA. Dollar amounts and savings will differ depending on income, state tax rules, city tax rules and other factors. Please consult a tax, legal or financial advisor about your own personal situation. If you are enrolled in a health flexible spending account (FSA), you should be aware of the rules around any unused dollars at the end of the Plan Year. The “Use It or Lose It” IRS Rule According to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), if you do not use all the money in your health FSA by the end of the Plan Year, you will lose the unused balance, unless you use it within the Grace Period . The grace period In the 2026 Plan Year, the Grace Period will be to March 15 after the Plan Year ends. This means that for the 2026 Plan Year, if you incur eligible health FSA expenses between January 1, 2026 and March 15, 2027, and you have a remaining balance in your 2026 health FSA, you will be reimbursed up to the remaining 2026 balance of your health FSA. In the 2027 Plan Year, the Grace Period will be to March 15 after the Plan Year ends, if you incur eligible health FSA expenses between January 1, 2027 and March 15, 2028 and you have a remaining balance in your 2027 health FSA, you will be reimbursed up to the remaining 2027 balance of your health FSA. 2026 Plan Year Deadline for Submitting Health FSA Claims For the Period of Coverage ending on December 31, 2026, the general deadline for submitting reimbursement forms to UnitedHealthcare is March 31, 2027 . However, if your Period of Coverage ends on any date prior to December 31, 2026, then the deadline for submitting reimbursement forms to UnitedHealthcare is 90 days after the date your Period of Coverage ends. For example, if your health FSA Period of Coverage ends on September 15, 2020, you will have until December 14, 2020 to submit your eligible health FSA claims in order to be reimbursed. If you need assistance calculating your specific deadline, contact the FSA Customer Care Center at 1-888-298-9754. IMPORTANT: Late claims cannot be paid. To receive reimbursement using any available 2026 Plan Year dollars, the reimbursement form must be either: Received by UnitedHealthcare by March 31, 2027 or, if applicable, 90 days after your Period of Coverage ends, or Mailed to UnitedHealthcare by first-class mail and postmarked on or before March 31, 2027, or, if applicable, 90 days after your Period of Coverage ends. Note: The IRS only allows you to be reimbursed from your health FSA for services received during the Plan Year. For example, you cannot use FSA dollars from a current Plan Year to pay for claims that took place in a prior Plan Year. Need personal assistance? data.content: What does that mean? Health FSA: A benefit plan that lets you put pre-tax dollars, which are deducted from your paycheck, into a special account to help pay for eligible medical, pharmacy, dental and vision expenses. Eligible expense: A medical, pharmacy, dental or vision expense that can be paid for or reimbursed from your health FSA. Learn more See the Frequently Asked Questions . Review additional health FSA information and tips . Watch the short video below to hear Alex’s insight about health FSAs. Need personal assistance? Call the FSA Customer Care Center at 1-888-298-9754 (8 a.m. - 8 p.m. EST). So, you have a health flexible spending account (FSA) but may not be quite sure when or even how to use it. This article should help clear things up and make it simpler to understand so you can make the most of your health FSA. What expenses can be paid for with your health FSA? Health FSA funds can be used to help pay for “qualified health FSA services or products.” The IRS decides specifically which expenses are qualified and which are not. Below are lists of some of the common eligible and ineligible items and services: Common eligible expenses: Acupressure Acupuncture Ambulance services Certain dental services Fertility treatments Hearing aids Insulin Laser eye surgery Over-the-counter medicines (OTC) and drugs if prescribed by a doctor (e.g., acid controllers, aids for indigestion, allergy or acne medicines, eye drops, aspirin, ibuprofen) Physical therapy Prescription drugs Walkers, wheelchairs, crutches and canes Common ineligible expenses: Aromatherapy Baby bottles, cups, wipes Breast enhancements Cosmetics Cotton swabs Dental floss Deodorants Feminine care Hair regrowth Low-calorie foods Mouthwash Petroleum jelly or baby oil Shampoo and conditioner Skin care Spa salts Sun-tanning products Toothbrushes These are not complete lists. See more FSA-eligible and -ineligible expenses here . The IRS and your employer may modify the list of eligible expenses from time to time so it’s important to keep up to date. Please see your benefit plan documents for the expenses that are eligible for reimbursement under your FSA. If you are unsure if an expense is eligible, call the FSA Customer Care Center at 1-888-298-9754 . How can you use your health FSA? There are several ways to use your health FSA dollars, including: Use your Health Care Spending Card from UnitedHealthcare. It’s that simple. You can use the card to pay for eligible FSA medical, dental, vision and pharmacy expenses by phone, the Web or any place that accepts MasterCard®. Your card is connected directly to your health FSA account. By using your card there is no need to write checks or submit an online or paper reimbursement form. Through automatic claims payment. Claim information for you and your enrolled dependents will automatically roll over from most of the Railroad’s benefit plan administrators* when they process a claim from a provider, hospital or pharmacy. Upon notification, any member responsibility owed on that claim for any eligible FSA expenses, such as deductible or co-payments, will be automatically deducted from your health FSA. No reimbursement forms or requests are necessary. The automatic payment feature is usually set to "on" when you start your health FSA plan year. To turn it off at any time or to ensure that it is set to on, go to myuhc.com ®, click on View Account Balances and select Automatic Payment Options . *Benefit plan administrators include Aetna, Highmark Blue Cross Blue Shield, UnitedHealthcare, Optum Rx, EyeMed and United Behavioral Health. Manually request reimbursement. You can submit claims and receipts for eligible health FSA expenses online at myuhc.com or with a paper reimbursement form . Your reimbursements can be deposited directly into your checking or savings account (sign up at myuhc.com ), or a check will be mailed to you. Remember to keep your receipts — you will need to include these when submitting for reimbursement.

data.title: Calories count in alcoholic beverages too
data.description: Alcohol has a lot of calories, often more than the dessert you turn down. And, having a drink or two before or with a meal may actually stimulate you to eat…
data.content: Think twice before taking that next drink Alcohol has a lot of calories, often more than the dessert you turn down. And, having a drink or two before or with a meal may actually stimulate you to eat more and take in more calories. As a result, you may gain extra pounds and add inches to your waistline. So, how many calories are in a drink? The calorie amounts listed here are for an average-sized drink. Many drinks may have even more, depending on the size of the tumbler, glass or beer mug. Drink Amount Calories Beer (regular) 12 oz. 150 Beer (light) 12 oz. 100 Daiquiri 10 oz. 300 Eggnog 8 oz. 350 Kahlua 1.5 oz. 140 Long Island Iced Tea 10 oz. 580 Martini 6 oz. 280 Margarita 8 oz. 420 Piña Colada 10 oz. 550 Screwdriver 8 oz. 190 Shot of Liquor (gin, rum, vodka, whiskey) 1.5 oz. 100 Whiskey Sour 8 oz. 375 White Russian 8 oz. 500 Wine (red or white) 6 oz. 120 If you choose to drink alcohol: Do so only in moderation. For healthy adults, that means up to one drink a day for women of all ages and men older than age 65, and up to two drinks a day for men ages 65 and younger. Check with your doctor if you take any medicines (over-the-counter or prescription) or if you have any medical problems. Pay attention to the calories. Some beer, wine and spirit containers may include a Serving Facts label that lists the serving size, calories, carbohydrate, fat and protein, and percent alcohol by volume values. Consider trading in a higher calorie drink for a lower one. Drink plenty of water. Your body is better able to process the alcohol when it’s properly hydrated. Never drink on an empty stomach. This will lead to faster absorption of the alcohol and even more impaired judgment. Learn to sip your drink to make it last longer. Don’t drink and drive. Alcohol interferes with a person’s coordination, driving skills and judgment, making driving especially dangerous. Plan ahead and arrange for a designated non-drinking driver to get you home safely. Get help if you think you have an alcohol addiction With your Railroad Behavioral Health benefits, you have 24-hour access to help, either toll-free or online. Call 1-866-850-6212 and talk with a specialist who can help you find the right resources, or Visit Live and Work Well (access code: Railroad) Be sure to discuss any health-related concerns with your doctor whenever you meet with him/her and also as part of your annual routine physical. data.title: Can you prevent prediabetes?
data.description: This is the second installment of a four-part series about prediabetes. Read part one to learn more about what prediabetes is and its risk factors. In the…
data.content: This is the second installment of a four-part series about prediabetes. Read part one to learn more about what prediabetes is and its risk factors. In the coming months, the third and fourth installments will be published to provide information about how prediabetes is diagnosed and other health risks that may be caused by the onset of prediabetes. Stay tuned! Understand your health and your risk Talk to your doctor about prediabetes and any other health concerns so you can understand your health risks and what you may be able to do to reduce them. Take advantage of the resources and support that are available as part of your Railroad benefits that can help you maintain and/or improve your overall health. For more information about these resources, contact your medical benefit administrator today: Aetna: Railroad Employees National Plan: 1-800-842-4044 NRC/UTU Plan: 1-888-332-8742 Highmark Blue Cross BlueShield: 1-866-267-3320 UnitedHealthcare: 1-866-735-5685 The answer is “yes.” By making healthy lifestyle changes to better manage your weight and overall health, you may be able to prevent or reverse prediabetes. 1 Prediabetes is a condition where your fasting blood glucose (sugar) 2 level is “ higher than normal ” but not yet high enough to be diagnosed as diabetes. Always seek the advice of a qualified physician or health provider for medical diagnosis and treatment. Consider healthier food choices. Having prediabetes or even diabetes doesn’t mean that you can no longer have sugar, or eat the certain foods that you may like. It’s more about controlling your portion size, cutting back on the size of sweets or baked goods, and reducing your intake of foods high in fat. Here are some tips to follow: Eat fewer fried foods. Try broiled or baked instead. Add more vegetables and fruits to your plate. Filling up on these can help reduce the amount of meat you consume. Choose more fish and chicken versus beef. If you want red meat, opt for lean cuts of beef , 3 like a sirloin steak or round roast. Think twice before taking that next drink. Alcohol has a lot of calories, often more than the dessert you turn down. If you choose to drink, understand alcohol calorie counts and consider smarter options. Stay active daily. Increasing your physical activity is a good idea in general but it’s even more important if you are at risk for prediabetes . Studies have shown that as little as two to three 15-minute activities a day can help lower your blood sugar. In addition to helping to prevent prediabetes, exercising regularly can help lower blood pressure and cholesterol, and it can help fight depression or anxiety . Connect with a Health Coach if you need support to get going and stay motivated (see side bar for contact information). Be sure to talk to your doctor about prediabetes and any other health concerns so you can understand your health risks and what you may be able to do to reduce them. data.title: Cholesterol: Are you on target?
data.description: High cholesterol is a major risk factor for heart disease, heart attacks, diabetes or other serious health conditions. It’s important to understand what…
data.content: Cholesterol: What are your numbers? What do they mean? High cholesterol is a major risk factor for heart disease, heart attacks, diabetes or other serious health conditions. It’s important to understand what cholesterol is, what your numbers are and what they mean, and what you can do to help improve any undesirable levels and/or maintain the good numbers. Types of cholesterol A blood test, called a lipid panel or lipid profile, is used to check three cholesterol levels: HDL cholesterol: high-density lipoprotein ("good" cholesterol). Helps prevent arteries from becoming clogged. This is the only cholesterol level where a higher number is a good thing–see the chart below. LDL cholesterol: low-density lipoprotein ("bad" cholesterol). Contributes to artery blockages that can lead to heart attacks. The lower your LDL, the better–see the numbers in the chart below. Triglycerides: a type of fat often increased by eating a diet high in carbohydrates, physical inactivity, smoking and excess alcohol consumption. Higher levels may increase the risk for heart disease and diabetes. Total cholesterol is calculated by adding HDL and LDL and 20% of the triglyceride level. How do your cholesterol numbers measure up? Adults ages 20 and older should have a lipid test to check their cholesterol levels. See the chart below for the desirable and undesirable cholesterol numbers by each type. Tips to lower your cholesterol Below are some things that may help you improve and/or maintain your numbers. Eat regular, well-balanced meals to avoid the urge to snack Eat white meat or lean cuts of red meat Remove skin and fat from chicken Use low-fat or no-fat dairy products, dressings and mayonnaise Increase your daily servings of fresh fruit, vegetables and grains (increase fiber) Limit or reduce added sugars and fructose Decrease or eliminate alcohol consumption Stay physically active Don’t smoke Maintain a healthy weight Keeping your cholesterol in check Talk with your doctor or health care provider to find out how often you should be tested, what your number goals should be based on your medical history and what you may be able to do to reach them. Your health plan also offers educational tools and resources (at no additional cost). These include health coaching, yourtracktohealth.com, a member website and a nurse help line. Check the back of your member ID card for the contact information for your member website and nurse help line. You can also visit mayoclinic.com or the American Heart Association for more information about cholesterol. The material contained in this article has been selected to provide general background and useful information regarding cholesterol. It is not designed to replace either medical advice or medical treatment. You should discuss the information, facts and tips with your doctor. You should not engage in physical activity, which may have injury and health risks associated with it, until you confirm with your doctor that it is appropriate for you. data.title: Cross-training: The benefits of mixing up your exercise activities
data.description: Support is available to help you get and stay on track with your health
data.content: Support is available to help you get and stay on track with your health Connect online and on the go There are hundreds of video demonstrations and mobile apps (many for free) available online that can to help you track and achieve your health goals. Exercise video demos for all fitness levels on YouTube (search: cross-training). topfitnessapps.com for reviews on some of the most popular fitness and health apps. Call a health coach As part of your Railroad benefits, a health coach can help you better understand exercise and nutrition. They are available to help you develop a plan so you can maintain or achieve better health. To connect with a health coach, contact your medical benefit administrator today: Aetna: Railroad Employees National Plan: 1-800-842-4044 NRC/UTU Plan: 1-888-332-8742 Highmark Blue Cross BlueShield: 1-866-267-3320 UnitedHealthcare: 1-866-735-5685 Some people just love to eat carrots. But, what if they were on your plate at every meal? Boredom aside, you’d miss out on essential nutrients that come from eating a variety of foods. Just as a diverse diet provides different but necessary vitamins and minerals, a complete exercise program should consist of varied activities to work every part of your body – in other words, cross-training . Cross-training means that you incorporate a variety of activities into your exercise routine. It’s a way to broaden your activities and work different muscles. For example, you may swim one day and run the next. Or, it can combine several types of exercises in one workout session. Remember to always check with your doctor before you increase your activity level. Cross-training may help you: Reduce the risk of injury. Overusing the same muscles and bones can potentially lead to injury. Varying your exercise routine gives part of your body time to rest while working other areas of your body. Enhance weight loss. If you want to lose weight, you need to burn a large number of calories. Doing more than one type of activity at a moderate level of intensity may help you reach your goal and keep you motivated. Improve overall fitness. Over time, cross-training may help lead to improved performance and increased endurance during activities. Stick with it. By adding some variety, you’ll probably have more fun and want to exercise more, especially if you’re doing things you enjoy. Mix up the activities, pace and place As you put together a routine, look for combinations of activities that are different from each other – and that use different muscles— to stay motivated and avoid burnout. For example, consider: Bicycling or swimming. They provide a low-impact aerobic workout. And, either is a great companion to weight-bearing exercise, such as running. Strength-training. According to experts, you should aim to do strength-training activities – such as lifting weights or doing push-ups – at least twice a week. They’re also a good way to break up your weekly exercise routine. For example, you could do aerobic exercise on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays. Then, you could strength train on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Flexibility and mindfulness exercises. Stretching exercises, like yoga or Pilates, can help build strength, keep you limber, and may help control and reduce stress. data.content: Diabetes and your eyes Did you know that if you have diabetes you’re at greater risk for eye problems that can lead to vision loss? In fact, diabetes is the leading cause of blindness in adults ages 20-74. An annual eye exam can lead to the early detection and treatment of diabetes, and also any serious vision-related complications caused by the disease, including: Glaucoma — If you have diabetes, you are 40 percent more likely to develop glaucoma, which may lead to irreversible vision loss . Cataracts — Diabetics are 60 percent more likely to develop cataracts. Cataracts cloud the eye’s lens, which blocks the passage of light , affecting your eyesight. Diabetic Retinopathy — This is the most common eye complication in diabetic patients and the leading cause of blindness. There are very slight and often unnoticeable symptoms of retinopathy. But there is good news: it may be treatable by laser surgery once detected. data.content: Prediabetes: How do I know if I have it? Understand your health and your risk Talk to your doctor about prediabetes and any other health concerns so you can understand your health risks and what you may be able to do to reduce them. Take advantage of the resources and support that are available as part of your Railroad benefits that can help you maintain and/or improve your overall health. For more information about these resources, contact your medical benefit administrator today: Aetna: Railroad Employees National Plan: 1-800-842-4044 NRC/UTU Plan: 1-888-332-8742 Highmark Blue Cross BlueShield: 1-866-267-3320 UnitedHealthcare 1-866-735-5685 Prediabetes is a condition where your blood glucose (sugar) level is “higher than normal” but not yet high enough to be diagnosed as diabetes (see the table below for more detail). Often, prediabetes has no signs or symptoms, so you may have it and not even know it. There are three tests that are commonly used to diagnose prediabetes: An A1C test , also called the hemoglobin A1c, HbA1c or glycohemoglobin test. Measures a person’s average blood glucose for the past two to three months. You can eat and drink normally before testing — fasting is not required.1 A fasting plasma glucose (FPG) test . To get an accurate measurement, no eating or drinking (except clear water) is allowed for at least 8 hours before this test is completed.1 An oral glucose tolerance test (also referred to as OGTT). This is a two-hour test. Blood glucose levels are measured before and then two hours after a person drinks a special sweet beverage (provided by a doctor) to indicate how their body processes glucose (sugar).1 Below is a chart2 on what the blood test results indicate by the type of test used: Any of these tests can be completed as part of your annual preventive check-up and involves getting a small sample of your blood to test. Adults, teens and children should be tested for prediabetes annually, or more often if needed, based on their risk factors . This is especially true if you’re age 45 or older, or are overweight at any age. If you are diagnosed with prediabetes, you should be screened for the onset of type 2 diabetes every one to two years, or more often, based on your risk factors. Be sure to talk with your doctor about which test is right for you and how often you should be tested based on your specific health status and risks. The silver lining: it may be possible to reverse prediabetes. By making healthy lifestyle changes, like eating healthier foods and staying active every day, you’ll be able to better manage your weight and overall health, and possibly reverse your prediabetes . data.title: Don’t get burned
data.description: Between the beach, the pool, and the weekend cookouts, you may be having too much fun to worry about sunburn – until that telltale stinging and redness set…
data.content: Don’t get burned! Between the beach, the pool, and the weekend cookouts, you may be having too much fun to worry about sunburn – until that telltale stinging and redness set in. Sunburn isn’t just painful – it’s also bad for your health. The dangers of sunburn The sun’s rays contain two types of ultraviolet light. Ultraviolet A (UVA) causes tanning, aging skin, and wrinkles. Ultraviolet B (UVB) causes sunburn. Both can cause skin cancer. You can burn on sunny days, cloudy days, and cold days. The white sand on the beach and the white snow of winter both reflect the sun’s rays. You can burn whether you’re skiing on water or snow. Signs of sunburn are redness and pain. You may also have swelling and blistering. A bad sunburn can lead to heatstroke and dehydration. Long-term effects Every time you tan or burn, DNA damage builds up in the deeper levels of your skin. Having 5 or more burns over a lifetime doubles your chances of getting skin cancer. Other side effects of tanning and burning include premature wrinkles and age (pigment) spots. Over time, the sun can age your skin, making it tough and leathery. Remember that your eyes can be affected, too. Too much sun can burn your corneas and lead to various eye diseases, including cataracts and age-related macular degeneration. These can cause vision loss. The truth about sunscreen Wearing sunscreen doesn’t always keep you from burning. No sunscreen can completely protect you from UV rays. A sunscreen labeled “waterproof” or “water resistant” will not protect you all day. When you swim or sweat, reapply your sunscreen. The UV index Your local news may broadcast daily UV index reports. The higher the index, the less time it will take to burn. Here is your risk for overexposure to the damaging UV rays. The number indicates the daily UV index, followed by the degree of risk. The higher the index on a given day, the greater the need to protect yourself. 0-2: low 3-5: moderate 6-8: high 8-10: very high 11+: extreme Preventing sunburn Use only water-resistant or waterproof sunscreen. It should protect against both UVA and UVB rays and have an SPF of at least 15. Reapply every 2 hours and after swimming or sweating. Wear protective clothing when possible. Always include a hat and sunglasses. Limit sun exposure between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. This is when UV rays are strongest. If your shadow is shorter than you are, get out of the sun. Keep children in the shade and in protective clothing. Follow the same sunscreen rules for them that you would for yourself. Don’t use sunscreen on children younger than 6 months old. They should be kept out of the sun. If a child under age 1 gets sunburn, call your pediatrician right away. Also seek emergency care if a child of any age has a sunburn with fever, blistering, severe pain, or lethargy. Be aware that water, snow, and sand all reflect UV rays and increase your chances for sunburn. Treatment Cool wet compresses, soothing lotions, and cool baths may help relieve minor sunburn pain. Drink plenty of fluids. For serious burns, call your doctor right away. Medication may prevent infection and help with the swelling and pain. Go to Top

data.title: Don’t let high blood pressure sneak up on you
data.description: Don’t let high blood pressure sneak up on you There are often no signs or symptoms associated with high blood pressure (hypertension). This could be…
data.content: Don’t fall victim to the “silent killer” Don’t let high blood pressure sneak up on you There are often no signs or symptoms associated with high blood pressure (hypertension). This could be silently damaging arteries, the heart and other organs — to men and women alike. If undetected or untreated, high blood pressure can lead to: Heart attack Stroke Kidney damage Blindness Erectile dysfunction Memory loss The good news is there are simple things you can do to help avoid this silent killer, starting with understanding the basics about blood pressure: It is recorded as two numbers, like this: 117/74. You might also hear this example described as “117 over 74.” - The first number is systolic pressure —the pressure in the arteries when your heart beats. - The second number is diastolic pressure —the pressure in the arteries between your heartbeats when the heart muscle is resting. A healthy blood pressure reading is 120/80 or less . High blood pressure is often genetic or inherited Do you know your blood pressure? Knowing your numbers is a very important step to take in protecting your health. You can have your blood pressure taken as part of your annual preventive care exam, at home with your own blood pressure monitor or at a local pharmacy (many pharmacies have do-it-yourself blood pressure stations). Five steps to healthier numbers Maintain a healthy weight. Losing as little as 5 to 10 pounds can make a big difference in your blood pressure. Ask your doctor what “healthy” means for you. Eat more plant-based foods. Think of your dinner plate (mindful of the size of the plate): 1/2 = vegetables and fruit 1/4 = lean protein like skinless chicken, fish, tofu or lean cuts of pork or beef (limiting sauces, gravies or dressings, which are usually high in fat content) 1/4 = carbohydrates (“starches”) such as sweet potatoes, whole-grain pasta or brown rice Pump up your physical activity. All you need are a couple of 15-minutes activities (such as a brisk walk or jog) each day to impact your blood pressure along with cholesterol. Bonus: exercise is also effective in helping with depression and anxiety. Manage stress. Take time during the day to relax, listen to music, practice yoga or simply sit quietly and meditate. If you prefer to burn off stress with physical activity , that can help too. Hold the salt. The recommended daily limit for sodium is 2,300 mg (roughly a single teaspoon), and most Americans consume between 4,000 to 6,000 mg on average per day. Make a habit of checking food labels for sodium, and add less salt at mealtimes. Know your blood pressure. Check it during your annual physical, at home on your own monitor, or at your local pharmacy or grocery store. Talk with your doctor at your annual exam or any other time you have questions about high blood pressure and any other health concerns. data.description: In less than 15 minutes a day, you can do a few simple and effective strengthening exercises that may help you set some health and wellness goals. These…
data.content: Too busy for a full work out? In less than 15 minutes a day, you can do a few simple and effective strengthening exercises that may help you set some health and wellness goals. These exercises should work the muscles in your legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders and arms. Below are some simple exercises that can be done just about anywhere. Check with your doctor before starting any exercise program or increasing your activity level — this is especially important if you have any health conditions (i.e. arthritis, diabetes, heart disease, pregnancy, neck, back or knee problems, etc.). He or she can tell you what types and amounts of activities are safe and suitable for you. Before you begin, it’s important to warm up. You can do this with a simple five-minute walk (walking in place counts). After you’re warmed up, do 8 to 12 repetitions of each exercise noted below for a complete set. When you’ve completed your first set, rest and then work your way up to a second or even third set as you are able and/or as time permits. If you experience any symptoms of weakness, unsteadiness, light-headedness or dizziness, chest pain or pressure, nausea, or shortness of breath while exercising, stop immediately and contact your doctor. If it is an emergency, call 911. Mild soreness after exercise may be experienced after beginning a new exercise. Contact your physician if the soreness does not improve after 2-3 days. Click here to print a handout of these exercises . Half squat Stand with your feet slightly wider than shoulder-width apart, with your arms straight out and parallel to the floor. As you go down, move your hips slightly forward and use your toes as a guide. Do not let your knees get in front of your toes. This will be easier if you place more weight on the heels of your feet than the balls or toes. Your back should be straight. Moving in a slow, controlled motion, bend your knees and hips until you reach a near-sitting position. Pause, then slowly push up to the starting position. Watch a demonstration of this exercise here . Forward lunge Stand with your feet together and engage your stomach muscles. Keeping your back straight, step one foot forward, shifting your body weight toward your lead foot. Lower your body toward your lead foot until your front thigh is parallel with the floor (your knee will be bent). Firmly push off with your lead leg, engaging both thighs and butt muscles, to return to the starting position. Note: This exercise can be done with or without hand weights. If you use weights, start with a light weight (i.e. 2 lbs.) and work your way up to more weight as you feel comfortable and gain strength. Reduce or eliminate the weights if you ever feel weakness, unsteadiness, light-headedness or dizziness, chest pain or pressure, nausea, or shortness of breath while using them. Watch a demonstration of this exercise here . Bent knee sit-up Lie on your back with feet flat on the floor. Place hands behind your head, elbows facing out. Slowly raise only your shoulders and upper back off the floor. Don’t rise all the way up. Exhale as you rise. Then slowly lower yourself, inhaling as you go. Do not pull on your neck or head and keep your chin pointed toward the ceiling. Watch a demonstration of this exercise here . Superman Lie on your stomach with your toes pointed behind you. Reach your arms over your head with your palms facing each other. Keep your neck relaxed and head down. Now lift both legs and both arms at the same time, raising your limbs a few inches off the floor. Keep both legs and both arms straight and hold. Slowly lower your legs and arms back to the starting position. Watch a demonstration of this exercise here . Toe raises Stand flat on the floor (use a countertop, chair or sturdy surface for balance, if needed) with your feet shoulder-width apart. Now raise your heels to stand on the balls of your feet as high as you can. Pause for 2 seconds and lower your heels to the floor. Watch a demonstration of this exercise here . Bent knee push-up Start on your hands and knees with your hands directly under your shoulders and your face looking forward. Next, engage your abdominal muscles, making sure your body forms a straight line from your head to your torso to your knees. Slowly bend your elbows and lower your body to the floor. Don’t let your back sag or your hips rise upward. Keep pressing down until your elbows are straight. Push up to the starting position. Watch a demonstration of this exercise here . data.title: Flu vaccines: Protect yourself and others
data.description: Each year, more than 200,000 people are hospitalized as a result of the flu, including an average of 20,000 children younger than five years of age. By…
data.content: Each year, more than 200,000 people are hospitalized as a result of the flu, including an average of 20,000 children younger than five years of age. By simply getting a seasonal flu vaccine, you can reduce your risk of getting the flu or possibly minimize the symptoms should you come down with the flu. Getting vaccinated can also protect the people around you who are more vulnerable to serious flu illness. Those at risk include: Older adults People with chronic health conditions, like asthma Pregnant women Young children, especially infants younger than six months old who are too young to get vaccinated Flu shots are covered by your medical plan at 100% when using an in-network provider* and when billed as preventive.** You can search your plan’s online provider directory to find a network provider in your area: Aetna members Highmark members UnitedHealthcare members *No coverage if the provider is out of network. **If the provider does not bill the vaccine and/or administration as preventive, then a co-pay or deductible and coinsurance may apply, depending on the plan you are enrolled in. Flu Vaccine FAQs Who should get a flu vaccine? It is recommended that everyone six months of age and older get vaccinated against the flu. When should I get a flu vaccine? Get vaccinated as soon as possible. The flu season peaks in January and February, so before December is best. However, the flu season can last as late as May, so getting vaccinated later in the flu season could still provide a protective benefit. Where can I get flu vaccines? Flu vaccines are offered in most doctor’s offices and clinics. If you don’t have a regular doctor or nurse, you can get a flu vaccine at a convenience care clinic. Can a flu shot give you the flu? No, flu shots are made either with inactive flu viruses or no viruses at all, and nasal spray flu vaccines are made with “weakened” flu viruses that can’t survive in the warm temperatures of our bodies. For more commonly asked questions and misperceptions about flu vaccines, go to http://www.cdc.gov/flu/about/qa/misconceptions.htm . data.title: Lyme disease
data.description: With summer finally here, it is important know about Lyme disease and how you can prevent it and treat it.
data.content: Lyme disease: Symptoms, prevention, treatment With summer finally here, it is important know about Lyme disease and how you can prevent it and treat it. What is Lyme disease? Lyme disease is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi and is transmitted to humans and animals through the bite of a deer tick or blacklegged tick. If left untreated, Lyme disease can cause: Chronic joint inflammation (Lyme arthritis), particularly of the knee Neurological symptoms, such as facial palsy and neuropathy Cognitive defects, such as impaired memory Heart rhythm irregularities Symptoms of Lyme disease The first sign of Lyme disease is often a rash where the tick bite occurred. The rash may start as a small red spot and get larger over a couple of days or weeks. The rash may be circular or oval-shaped and may look like a bull’s eye. As the infection spreads, the rash can appear on different areas on the body. Along with the rash, you may also experience flu-like symptoms: headache fever body aches stiff neck fatigue Preventing Lyme disease Here are some useful tips to prevent Lyme disease: Avoid tick-infested areas. This includes wooded areas and shady grasslands where ticks are common. Cover up. Wear long pants, sleeves and socks to keep ticks off your skin. Use a tick repellent on yourself, your children and your pets. You can find an effective tick repellent containing permethrin at most lawn and garden stores. Check for ticks on yourself, your children and your pets. Be sure to check the hairy areas of the body and wash all clothing once you are back inside. Removing ticks If you find a tick, remove it by using fine-tipped tweezers; do not use petroleum jelly, a hot match, nail polish or other products. Make sure all parts of the tick are removed, and clean the area with rubbing alcohol or soap and water. Treatment of Lyme disease If you have been, or think you have been bitten by a tick and have any of the symptoms listed above, see your doctor as soon as possible. Your doctor can do an exam and order tests to diagnosis if you have Lyme disease. If diagnosed, you may be prescribed antibiotics. A complete recovery from Lyme disease is possible with appropriate treatment. data.title: Portion distortion: What is a normal serving size?

data.content: One of the biggest challenges to weight management is related to food portion size. Portion size has grown so much in recent decades, it’s hard to even imagine what a normal serving looks like. In many popular restaurants and fast-food chains, the cost difference between the regular size options and the supersize options often creates a perception that the “value is better when you go big.” The downside is that this can cause you to consume more calories than the daily amount needed, resulting in excessive weight gain. This may lead to prediabetes and/or diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and other serious health problems. Become a “portion pro” If you know what a healthy portion size should be, you will be able to make smarter choices whenever you’re preparing your plate or selecting a snack. Use the serving size guide to the right to better understand what a “healthy” portion size should look like. Click on the image to open up a printable version of the pocket guide to carry with you wherever you eat, including at home, at a friend’s home, at the office, on the go or at a restaurant. Right-size your portions Here are a few additional tips to help aid in eating healthier and right-sizing your portions: Resist the urge to “super-size” any item. Avoid “combo” meals. Think “half”…half a sandwich, half a wrap, half an entrée or half a portion when available. Read food labels and pay attention to the actual serving size and servings per package, especially on “snack size” packages. The servings per package may actually be for more than one serving, which means you should only be eating a portion of the bag. When dining with a friend, consider ordering one meal and sharing it. Order a “cup” instead of a “bowl.” Despite what your parents may have taught you, you don’t have to finish everything on your plate. data.description: This is the first of a four-part series about prediabetes. Stay tuned for future communications in the coming months that will focus on lifestyle changes…
data.content: This is the first of a four-part series about prediabetes. Stay tuned for future communications in the coming months that will focus on lifestyle changes that may help prevent prediabetes, how prediabetes is diagnosed, and other health risks that may be caused by the onset of prediabetes. Understand your health and your risk Talk to your doctor about prediabetes and any other health concerns so you can understand your health risks and what you may be able to do to reduce them. Take advantage of the resources and support that are available as part of your Railroad benefits that can help you maintain and/or improve your overall health. For more information about these resources, contact your medical benefit administrator today: Aetna: Railroad Employees National Plan: 1-800-842-4044 NRC/UTU Plan: 1-888-332-8742 Highmark Blue Cross BlueShield: 1-866-267-3320 UnitedHealthcare: 1-866-735-5685 What is prediabetes? You may know about type 2 diabetes, but what about prediabetes? Prediabetes means that your fasting blood sugar 1 level is "higher than normal." A fasting blood sugar test is conducted after you have not eaten anything for at least 8 hours. Fasting blood sugar indicator levels are: 2 Under 100 mg/dl: Normal (healthy) 100-125 mg/dl: Prediabetes (higher than normal) 126 mg/dl and above: Diabetes Always seek the advice of a qualified physician or health provider for medical diagnosis and treatment. Who is at risk for getting prediabetes? The exact cause of prediabetes is unknown, but researchers have found that excess body weight — especially in the abdominal area — and inactivity are common factors in those that have prediabetes. Risk factors that can increase the likelihood of prediabetes include: 3 Family history of type 2 diabetes Excess weight ( Body Mass Index over 25) 4 Lack of activity/exercise Age 45 or older High blood pressure HDL cholesterol (the “good” cholesterol) is below 35 milligrams or your triglyceride level is above 250 milligrams Ethnicity is African-American, Hispanic, American Indian, Asian-American or a Pacific Islander Gestational diabetes during pregnancy, or your baby's birth weight was over 9 pounds Sleeping fewer than six hours or more than nine hours a night What are the symptoms? Often, prediabetes has no signs or symptoms. One symptom you may notice is darkened skin around the neck, armpits, elbows, knees and knuckles. This is a condition called acanthosis nigricans and is one of the few visible signs that you may be at risk for prediabetes. 3 How will prediabetes affect me? If you are diagnosed with prediabetes, it may be a time to consider making lifestyle changes to improve your overall health. With healthy lifestyle changes — such as eating healthy foods, exercising and maintaining your weight, blood pressure and cholesterol levels — you may be able to bring your blood sugar level back to normal. Without these changes, prediabetes is likely to become type 2 diabetes within 10 years or less. And, if you have prediabetes, the long-term damage of diabetes — especially to your heart and circulatory system — may already be starting. 3 This material has been selected to provide background and useful information. data.title: Prioritizing A1C tests can help keep diabetes in check
data.description: If you have diabetes or prediabetes, there are many helpful steps you can take to manage your health, including being active, eating a nutritious diet,…
data.content: If you have diabetes or prediabetes, there are many helpful steps you can take to manage your health, including being active, eating a nutritious diet, taking your medications, seeing a doctor regularly and more. One of the most important steps you can take is getting an A1C test every 6 months . What is an A1C test? An A1C test is a blood test that shows what your average blood glucose (sugar) level has been over the past few months. An A1C test can identify prediabetes, which raises your risk for diabetes, and it can also be used to diagnose diabetes. What does A1C stand for? A1C refers to hemoglobin A1C, which is a protein in your red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to the cells. When your blood sugar is high, more sugar attaches to the hemoglobin. An A1C test measures how much sugar has attached to your hemoglobin. Why is it important to get an A1C test? Your A1C level shows how well your diabetes is being managed. A higher A1C reading indicates a higher blood sugar level. A lower reading would mean your blood sugar levels are likely under control. What is a good A1C reading? Your doctor can help you set a goal based on your age, health and personal situation. For most adults with diabetes, the goal is an A1C of less than 7%. * How often do I need an A1C test? If your diabetes is under control and you’re at your target A1C level, you should generally be tested twice a year. Your doctor can discuss your results with you and adjust your treatment plan, if necessary. * Are A1C tests covered by my plan? Yes. The National Railroad Plans – Health & Welfare Benefits provide access to a wide range of resources for managing diabetes, including coverage for A1C tests. Act now to stay on track with your A1C testing. If it’s been more than 6 months since your last A1C test, contact your doctor to schedule one today. data.title: Protect your eyes from UV rays
data.description: Ultraviolet (UV) rays of the sun — a serious risk not only to your skin The intense UV rays of the sun can damage sensitive cells in the eyes, eventually…
data.content: Your eyes: protect them from the sun’s UV rays Ultraviolet (UV) rays of the sun — a serious risk not only to your skin The intense UV rays of the sun can damage sensitive cells in the eyes, eventually affecting vision. Unprotected, repeated exposure of UV rays may lead to serious eye problems later in life, including cataracts (a clouding of the lens), pterygium (a growth on the surface) and cancerous tumors on the skin around the eyes. Cataracts are a leading cause of reduced vision in the United States in people age 60 and older, according to the National Eye Institute. While it may take years before you experience any of the above-mentioned problems, there is risk of damage that can occur in the short term , including photokeratitis and photoconjunctivitis. Both are an inflammation of the eye as a result of extreme UV exposure and can be very painful during the healing process (think peeling/sensitive skin after a sunburn). Sources of UV exposure Although direct sunlight from the sun itself is extremely damaging to eyes, indirect reflected UV rays from the ground can be even more dangerous . Snow is one of the most dangerous indirect sources of UV and may cause snow blindness, which can lead to more serious complications such as chronic eye irritations or tearing. The table below shows the UV radiation reflection levels for several common indirect sources. The higher the percent, the more risk of eye damage. Surface UV reflection Grass, Open Water 2-8% Asphalt 4-9% Light-colored concrete 8-12% Dry beach or sand 15-18% Sea surf/sea foam 25-30% Snow Up to 80% Protect your eyes and your children’s eyes While sunglasses are definitely a good idea when it comes to eye protection, not all sunglasses are created equal. It’s highly recommended that you choose sunglasses that limit transmission to no more than 1 percent of UV rays. When purchasing sunglasses for you and your children: Look for a label on the lenses that indicates 99 percent of the UV rays are blocked. Consider wraparound sunglasses or lenses large enough to completely cover the eye and to help prevent as much light as possible from entering through the edges of the glasses. Consider darker lenses, particularly if you are more light-sensitive. Gray lenses provide the least color distortion but do not offer any better protection than other colored lenses. There are also UV-blocking contact lenses for added protection. Talk to your eye care professional for more information about UV-blocking contact lenses. More is better when it comes to protecting your eyes from the sun. If you’re planning to be out in the sun, protect your eyes with a combination of quality sunglasses, UV-blocking contact lenses (if you wear contacts) and a wide-brimmed hat. Talk to your eye care professional who can help you choose the right eyewear so you can enjoy the great outdoors even more. data.content: Tips for staying on Your Track to Health when travel is required When you have to be away from home, out of routine and without access to your gym or equipment, it might be easy to justify skipping exercise or healthy eating. Here are some simple and practical tips to help you stay on track with your health. Plan ahead and schedule the time Review your travel itinerary and schedule time on your calendar to work in an aerobic or strength routine each day, if possible. Studies have shown that as little as two to three 15-minute activities can benefit you just as much as a longer, single session. No gym, no equipment — no excuse! Walk: Park far from entrances so you have a good walk to the entrance. Skip the taxi when you’re within walking distance to your destination. Use the stairs instead of the escalator or elevator. Explore local parks and trails. Visit county and city websites for maps and information about the area. Use your own body as “equipment and weight”: Try jumping jacks, push-ups, squats, crunches, stair climbing (the real ones) and side bends (see side bar). Watch this 10-minute no-equipment-necessary workout video . Find more workouts and exercises that don’t require equipment by searching YouTube . Don’t forget about eating healthy while on the go Don’t skip meals: Regular meals can help stave off hunger and prevent you from overeating at any one meal, snack or dessert. Snack healthy: Fruit, yogurt, veggies, whole-grain crackers and low-fat cheese are good options. Balance what you eat and when: If you indulge for one meal, choose lower-calorie foods for your other meals. Use mobile apps to help manage and track your activities There are hundreds of mobile apps —many for free— available to help you stay on track with your exercise and fitness goals. Check out topfitnessapps.com for reviews on some of the most popular fitness and health apps. You can find more by visiting your mobile app store and searching by fitness, exercise or a specific activity (e.g., running, exercise tracker, weight loss, etc.). data.content: Not all dietary fats are bad for your diet. There are “better” fats, known as monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats. These fats are important in providing your body with energy, supporting cell growth, protecting your organs and helping to keep your body warm. When eaten in moderation, they can be an important part of a healthy diet. On the flip side, there are “bad” fats, also known as saturated and trans fats. These are the kind of fats that are not necessary in your diet and offer no nutritional value. How much fat do you need in your daily diet? Your daily limit of fat grams depends on your daily total calorie needs. Your daily total calorie needs depends on your age, gender, height, current weight and daily activity style (i.e., sedentary, moderately active, very active, etc.). Generally, the amount of recommended fat as a percent of your daily calories is: Total fat : Less than 25–35% Saturated fat : Less than 10% Trans fat : Less than 1% Use the online calorie calculator tool from the Mayo Clinic to quickly calculate your recommended daily calorie needs. The nutrition labels on foods can also be helpful when you’re shopping and making choices to help you understand specific calories and fat values. data.title: Everyday mental health
data.description: There’s a lot of advice about parenting out there, and it can feel overwhelming. If you’re looking for ways to help the young people in your life be…
data.content: Practical tips for parents There’s a lot of advice about parenting out there, and it can feel overwhelming. If you’re looking for ways to help the young people in your life be mentally and emotionally healthy, skip the noise and try these easy tips. Age 3–6 As kids start preschool, they can become more curious. It’s a great time to help them learn to talk about emotions. Find little moments to connect. Read a book, color or do an art project together. Play a matching game or card game like Go Fish together. Be smart about screen time. If you’re going to allow screen time, watch with your child, or preview programs and sites ahead of time. 1 Look for educational content that encourages participation, creativity and problem-solving. 1 Be a good listener. Encourage kids to share their feelings, using words like sad, mad, happy or worried. Don’t question them right at school or daycare pickup. Give them time to open up. Age 7–12 Throughout elementary and middle school, kids start to focus more on their peers. They can be concerned about fitting in. Find little moments to connect. Set aside time to do a puzzle, build a playlist or play a board game together. Follow their lead. For example, if they like music or sports, find ways to do it together. Be smart about screen time. If you choose to give them a smartphone, set limits. The American Academy of Pediatrics doesn’t recommend social media for kids under 13. 2 Model healthy behavior. Set your phone down so you can pay attention to others and create screen-free zones, such as the dinner table and bedroom. Be a good listener. Invite them to join you in making dinner, running errands or doing other everyday tasks. These little moments can spark great conversation. Make talking about feelings and mental health common in your home. Share how you’re feeling and invite them to do the same. Age 13–26 Between puberty and social pressures, the teen years can be tough. Teens want to establish their own identity, yet they still need their parents’ guidance. The transition to adulthood can be exciting, but it comes with big changes that can sometimes feel scary, for both parents and their children. Find little moments to connect. Invite them to join activities you’re already doing, such as a DIY project or cooking dinner. Once your child moves away, make time for phone or video calls and be sure to give them your full attention. Be smart about screen time. Discuss healthy boundaries on social media and talk about how social media makes them feel. Teach them to think critically. Remember that not everything on the internet can be trusted. Be a good listener. Don’t try to solve their problems unless they ask you to. Sometimes, we all just want someone to listen. Remember that teens and young adults are growing into independence. Be there when they need you, but don’t micromanage them. All ages Remind your child you’re here for them. Tell them that you care and will always be available to support them when they don’t feel good—in their mind or their body. Know where to go for support. If you’re looking for extra support, check out this flyer to learn all that’s available to you and your family as part of your National Railroad Plans – Health & Welfare Benefits. data.description: Understand heart disease risk factors, the 4 health risk numbers to know, questions for your doctor, and heart-healthy programs available with your Railroad benefits.
data.content: A guide to understanding heart disease risk factors — and learning ways to help your heart to better health. Take control of your heart health As the hardest-working muscle in your body, your heart is essential for nearly everything that keeps it healthy — from pumping blood to delivering oxygen and nutrients to your cells. Improving your heart health may have long-term benefits for your overall well-being. Use this guide to learn about common risks for heart disease, how to reduce those risks and steps to move you toward a heart-healthier lifestyle. A closer look at heart disease Heart disease — also known as cardiovascular disease — is the top cause of death in the U.S. It prevents the heart from pumping blood the way it should. That means blood may have trouble getting to the heart, lungs and other organs. Common risk factors Anyone can develop heart disease, but you may be more at risk if you have certain health conditions. Take heart, though: Some risk factors can be controlled, and it may be possible to prevent, stabilize or even improve some of the causes of heart disease. Diabetes Diabetes and heart disease often go hand-in-hand — because, over time, high blood sugar levels can harm blood vessels and the nerves that control the heart. People with diabetes are 2 times more likely to have a heart attack or stroke. Keeping blood sugar in a healthy range may help fend off some of that extra risk. High blood pressure High blood pressure can do damage throughout the body and may raise the risk of heart failure, kidney disease, blindness and more. One slightly above-normal reading may not be a problem. But when readings on 2 or more occasions are elevated, it may be a concern — and a signal for action. High cholesterol It’s normal to have some cholesterol. But if levels aren’t on target, the stage can be set for clogged arteries — and a heart attack or stroke. Having your cholesterol checked is a good way to know where you stand. Overweight or obesity Carrying around extra pounds may take a toll on the heart — and may raise the risk of heart disease. Losing even a modest amount of weight — 5–7% of your weight — may help improve health. Physical inactivity People who are inactive are nearly twice as likely to develop heart disease as those who are active. Aerobic exercise benefits the heart and lungs the most, but even modest amounts of physical activity are good for health. Generally speaking, most adults should aim for at least 2.5 hours a week of moderate aerobic physical activity* — such as taking a walk, raking the yard or swimming. Smoking Quitting smoking is one of the most important things people can do to help reduce their risk for heart disease. People who smoke are 2 to 4 times more likely to develop heart disease than nonsmokers. The good news is that as soon as someone quits smoking, their risk begins to go down — and continues to decrease over time. Get to know these 4 health risk numbers Health risk number Target number Blood pressure Less than 120 over 80 Total cholesterol 200 or less HDL (good) cholesterol** Above 40 men/50 women LDL (bad) cholesterol*** Below 100 Glucose (blood sugar) Between 70 and 100 Body Mass Index (BMI) Between 18.5 and 24.9 Targets established by National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute. * Talk with your doctor before significantly increasing your activity level. ** High-density lipoprotein (HDL), sometimes called “good” cholesterol. *** Low-density lipoprotein (LDL), sometimes called “bad” cholesterol. Have a heart-to-heart with your primary doctor Taking care of your heart is important to your overall health. A good way to learn about heart disease risk factors is by getting in touch with your primary doctor. A primary doctor may also be called a primary care provider (PCP). They know your health history and health goals — and can help you learn ways to protect your heart’s health. Need a PCP? Contact your individual medical plan or reach out to the 24/7 Nurses & Health Specialists for assistance at 1-866-735-5685. Questions to start the conversation Here are some important heart-health questions you might ask your primary doctor at your next checkup: “What should my blood pressure be? How often should it be checked?” “Should I be screened for diabetes? What should my blood sugar level be?” “What should my cholesterol and triglyceride levels be? How often should they be checked?” “Can you suggest any resources that could help me lose weight or stop smoking?” “What lifestyle changes would you recommend for me?” “What’s a healthy weight for me?” “How can I make sure I’m taking my prescription medications the right way? And what should I do if I’m having side effects?” Recommended preventive care An annual physical is a great opportunity to talk to a doctor about risk factors and what screenings may be right for you. data.content: Return to Home Page This is the first of a four-part series about prediabetes. Stay tuned for future communications in the coming months that will focus on lifestyle changes that may help prevent prediabetes, how prediabetes is diagnosed, and other health risks that may be caused by the onset of prediabetes. Understand your health and your risk Talk to your doctor about prediabetes and any other health concerns so you can understand your health risks and what you may be able to do to reduce them. Take advantage of the resources and support that are available as part of your Railroad benefits that can help you maintain and/or improve your overall health. For more information about these resources, contact your medical benefit administrator today: Aetna: Railroad Employees National Plan: 1-800-842-4044 NRC/UTU Plan: 1-888-332-8742 Highmark Blue Cross BlueShield: 1-866-267-3320 UnitedHealthcare: 1-866-735-5685 What is prediabetes? You may know about type 2 diabetes, but what about prediabetes? Prediabetes means that your fasting blood sugar 1 level is "higher than normal." A fasting blood sugar test is conducted after you have not eaten anything for at least 8 hours. Fasting blood sugar indicator levels are: 2 Under 100 mg/dl: Normal (healthy) 100-125 mg/dl: Prediabetes (higher than normal) 126 mg/dl and above: Diabetes Always seek the advice of a qualified physician or health provider for medical diagnosis and treatment. Who is at risk for getting prediabetes? The exact cause of prediabetes is unknown, but researchers have found that excess body weight — especially in the abdominal area — and inactivity are common factors in those that have prediabetes. Risk factors that can increase the likelihood of prediabetes include: 3 Family history of type 2 diabetes Excess weight ( Body Mass Index over 25) 4 Lack of activity/exercise Age 45 or older High blood pressure HDL cholesterol (the “good” cholesterol) is below 35 milligrams or your triglyceride level is above 250 milligrams Ethnicity is African-American, Hispanic, American Indian, Asian-American or a Pacific Islander Gestational diabetes during pregnancy, or your baby's birth weight was over 9 pounds Sleeping fewer than six hours or more than nine hours a night What are the symptoms? Often, prediabetes has no signs or symptoms. One symptom you may notice is darkened skin around the neck, armpits, elbows, knees and knuckles. This is a condition called acanthosis nigricans and is one of the few visible signs that you may be at risk for prediabetes. 3 How will prediabetes affect me? If you are diagnosed with prediabetes, it may be a time to consider making lifestyle changes to improve your overall health. With healthy lifestyle changes — such as eating healthy foods, exercising and maintaining your weight, blood pressure and cholesterol levels — you may be able to bring your blood sugar level back to normal. Without these changes, prediabetes is likely to become type 2 diabetes within 10 years or less. And, if you have prediabetes, the long-term damage of diabetes — especially to your heart and circulatory system — may already be starting. 3 This material has been selected to provide background and useful information. It is not designed to replace either medical advice or medical treatment.
