data.title: Can you prevent prediabetes?
data.description: This is the second installment of a four-part series about prediabetes. Read part one to learn more about what prediabetes is and its risk factors. In the…
data.content: Return to Home Page This is the second installment of a four-part series about prediabetes. Read part one to learn more about what prediabetes is and its risk factors. In the coming months, the third and fourth installments will be published to provide information about how prediabetes is diagnosed and other health risks that may be caused by the onset of prediabetes. Stay tuned! Understand your health and your risk Talk to your doctor about prediabetes and any other health concerns so you can understand your health risks and what you may be able to do to reduce them. Take advantage of the resources and support that are available as part of your Railroad benefits that can help you maintain and/or improve your overall health. For more information about these resources, contact your medical benefit administrator today: Aetna: Railroad Employees National Plan: 1-800-842-4044 NRC/UTU Plan: 1-888-332-8742 Highmark Blue Cross BlueShield: 1-866-267-3320 UnitedHealthcare: 1-866-735-5685 The answer is “yes.” By making healthy lifestyle changes to better manage your weight and overall health, you may be able to prevent or reverse prediabetes. 1 Prediabetes is a condition where your fasting blood glucose (sugar) 2 level is “ higher than normal ” but not yet high enough to be diagnosed as diabetes. Always seek the advice of a qualified physician or health provider for medical diagnosis and treatment. Consider healthier food choices. Having prediabetes or even diabetes doesn’t mean that you can no longer have sugar, or eat the certain foods that you may like. It’s more about controlling your portion size, cutting back on the size of sweets or baked goods, and reducing your intake of foods high in fat. Here are some tips to follow: Eat fewer fried foods. Try broiled or baked instead. Add more vegetables and fruits to your plate. Filling up on these can help reduce the amount of meat you consume. Choose more fish and chicken versus beef. If you want red meat, opt for lean cuts of beef , 3 like a sirloin steak or round roast. Think twice before taking that next drink. Alcohol has a lot of calories, often more than the dessert you turn down. If you choose to drink, understand alcohol calorie counts and consider smarter options. Stay active daily. Increasing your physical activity is a good idea in general but it’s even more important if you are at risk for prediabetes . Studies have shown that as little as two to three 15-minute activities a day can help lower your blood sugar. In addition to helping to prevent prediabetes, exercising regularly can help lower blood pressure and cholesterol, and it can help fight depression or anxiety . Be sure to talk to your doctor about prediabetes and any other health concerns so you can understand your health risks and what you may be able to do to reduce them. data.title: Ten straight answers to COVID-19 vaccine questions
data.description: Information about the COVID-19 vaccine can be confusing. It’s important to remember that vaccines save lives, protecting people from harmful diseases like…
data.content: Date: 3/8/2021 Information about the COVID-19 vaccine can be confusing. It’s important to remember that vaccines save lives, protecting people from harmful diseases like polio and smallpox—which are no longer a threat in the U.S. because people were vaccinated. 1 The combination of getting vaccinated and following recommendations from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) offers the best protection from COVID-19 for people across the country and in the communities we call home. 2 The COVID-19 vaccine was developed so fast. Is it safe? Yes, it is safe. Even though this vaccine was developed quickly, precautions were not overlooked. After large clinical trials to test safety and effectiveness, scientists confirmed the vaccines meet the strict standards set by the Food & Drug Administration (FDA). 3 Can the COVID-19 vaccine give you COVID-19? No, you can’t get COVID-19 from the vaccine. Vaccines give you the ability to fight off the virus if you are exposed to COVID-19, so you don’t get sick (or as sick as you would without getting vaccinated). 4 What are the side effects of the vaccine? Some people may have mild or moderate reactions—such as a headache, fever or muscle pain—which usually go away in a few days. NOTE: Despite what you might see on social media, the vaccine is not being used to gather personal information and it will not alter your DNA. 5 Why does everyone need to get vaccinated? It’s important because vaccinations help us develop “herd immunity” to help stop the spread, rather than allowing the disease to infect people, which could result in unnecessary deaths. Vaccinating a large portion of the population helps to safely achieve herd immunity. 6 Which vaccine is better (and can I choose)? The vaccines approved for use in the U.S. are safe and effective at preventing COVID-19 infection, and any available option is better than no shot at all. Be sure to follow vaccine guidelines, including getting a second shot (if required). Due to limited availability, a choice of vaccines may not be available. 7 If i’ve had COVID-19, do I still need to get vaccinated? Having COVID-19 may give you some natural immunity for a time, but we’re still not sure how long it will last. Because there’s still much we don’t know and cases of re-infection have been reported, it’s better to be safe by getting vaccinated. 4 Are there people who shouldn’t get vaccinated? Yes, people who’ve had a severe or immediate allergic reaction to a COVID-19 vaccine or one of its ingredients should not receive that vaccine. They may be eligible to get a different COVID-19 vaccine, and should be observed for 30 minutes after receiving it. People who have had an allergic reaction to other injectable medications may be eligible to be vaccinated, but with precautions. If you’re not sure whether you should be vaccinated, talk to your doctor. 8 Where do I go to get vaccinated? Because supplies are limited, each state has its own vaccination priority plan. For information about when and where you can get vaccinated, visit your state health department website. Find the link to your state at cdc.gov/publichealthgateway/healthdirectories/healthdepartments.html . How much does a vaccination cost? During the public health emergency, the vaccine is available at $0 cost—no matter where you get vaccinated, you will not pay a copay, deductible, coinsurance or any administrative costs for either of the two doses that are required. * What can I do to protect myself from the new COVID-19 variants? The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends taking the same precautions you’ve been taking during the pandemic: avoid crowds, stay home if you’re sick and wear a face mask that fits snugly over your nose and mouth—layering masks is recommended for extra protection. 9 Learn more Need more information? 24/7 Nurses & Health Specialists can help. Whether you’re wondering what priority group you may be in for vaccinations, or you want to know how to get vaccinated in your state and what to expect, specialists are standing by to answer your questions. Call 24/7 Nurses & Health Specialists at 1-866-735-5685. For the latest information, visit cdc.gov and click “How to Get a COVID-19 Vaccine.” * If you get vaccinated during a regular office visit, the visit will be covered according to your medical plan benefits. 1 World Health Organization. who.int/news-room/facts-in-pictures/detail/immunization . How the health FSA works A health flexible spending account (FSA) lets you put pre-tax dollars deducted from your paycheck into a special account to help pay for eligible medical, pharmacy, dental and vision expenses. View a list of eligible expenses . You’ll pay for eligible expenses using a Health Care Spending Card that’s connected to your FSA. You can contribute any amount from $10 per month ($120 annually) up to $283.33 per month ($3,400 annually). If the IRS raises the maximum for 2027, you’ll be able to elect up to that amount. After you’ve enrolled, you’ll be able to manage the account online at myuhc.com ® . Save money Your health FSA contributions are pre-tax.
